A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same oRGrad research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial rewriting and repagination.

before.justification: Section 8 reports original synthetic convergence, noise-sensitivity and fixed-step regret experiments, plus MovieLens evaluation results.

after.justification: Section 8 retains the original simulations and MovieLens results and adds an adaptive-step regret experiment.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same single-observation Riemannian update, HOSVD retraction, and adaptive schedule that halves step sizes while doubling phase lengths. Naming and theoretical-condition changes do not introduce a new procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic tensor regression, tensor completion, matrix regression for regret, and MovieLens matrix completion. The added adaptive experiment uses the retained matrix-regression task; broader theoretical design assumptions do not establish new empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Section 8.3 now compares the fixed-step procedure with the already-defined adaptive-oRGrad variant through Figure 2; v1 reports only the fixed-step simulation. The MovieLens comparator remains offline RGrad from Wei et al. (2016).

E3.justification: The added regret experiment evaluates Algorithm 2's adaptive schedule alongside the retained fixed-step setting. The reported 30-by-30 rank-two matrix, noise level 0.2, and horizons from 5,000 to 200,000 remain unchanged, as do the other experiments' settings.

E4.justification: Figure 2 adds an analysis of whether adaptive step sizes produce logarithmic regret growth, extending v1's fixed-step growth analysis. The step-size and noise-sensitivity analyses in Figure 1 are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten independent trials for the noise-level error-bar plots in Figure 1. The added regret curve supplies no new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or statistical testing practice.

E6.justification: Figure 2 adds adaptive-regret results showing approximately linear growth against log(T). Fixed-step magnitudes also change: at T=200,000, v1 plots squared regret around 1.05 billion, implying regret around 32,000, whereas v2 plots regret around 240,000. This discrepancy exceeds an axis transformation and is unexplained. Figure 1 and Table 2 results are unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces isotropic sub-Gaussian design with a broader bounded-covariance assumption. Theorems 7–8 extend stated guarantees to noisy completion, and Theorem 8 strengthens the initial-phase-length requirement. Theorem 5 removes the separate Frobenius-error SNR condition. Section 6 changes the regret definition and indexing, Section 5 changes an error factor from gamma_alpha^-2 to gamma_alpha^-1, and Appendix D.5 revises the adaptive-regret recursion. Most other appendix mathematics is retained.

C1.justification: The central algorithm, trade-off, incoherence and adaptive logarithmic-regret contributions remain. V2 withdraws the abstract's description of fixed-step square-root regret as optimal and broadens the stated regret guarantees to completion. Its new contribution (f) impossibility claim conflicts with Section 7's simultaneous-optimality claim.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds an SNR-dependent qualification: the regret comparison is optimal up to dimension logarithms at constant SNR, while general-SNR optimality concerns dependence on T. Conversely, contribution (f) newly asserts that statistical and regret optimality cannot coexist, contradicting Section 7. Section 3.2 also drops v1's explicit matrix-only qualification when matching the cited logistic-regression lower bound.

D1.justification: Simulation construction, initialization methods, existing numerical settings, and MovieLens processing and access information are retained. The added adaptive experiment references the existing Algorithm 2 without supplying experiment-specific initial step-size or phase-length values or additional implementation resources.

R1.justification: V2 adds Zhang (2004) and removes Anzai (2012), Liao and Chin (2007), Bastani and Bayati (2020), and Goldenshluger and Zeevi (2013), including the earlier forced-sampling inspiration attribution. Logarithmic-regret novelty is reframed from nonconvex functions generally to high-dimensional online learning.

P1.justification: The abstract and extensive passages in Sections 3–7 are rewritten and condensed. Repeated linear-regression explanations are removed, numbered theorem remarks become thematic paragraphs, duplicate assumptions are consolidated, and the separate Section 7.1 heading disappears. This is substantial editorial restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from one squared-regret-versus-horizon plot to two panels showing regret against square-root horizon and log horizon, with revised axes and caption. Figure 1 and both tables retain their displays; remaining visual changes mainly involve reflow and equation numbering.

improvement.justification: V2 removes substantial repetition and adds useful empirical support for adaptive logarithmic regret. However, it introduces conflicting simultaneous-optimality claims and changes Section 6's comparator supremum to an infimum that is inconsistent with its prediction-error definition. Appendix D.5 replaces an unfinished argument, but its displayed recursion does not justify the newly claimed 4^-k decay alongside a 2^-k noise term. These unresolved issues in the central theory prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
